strengths: The paper addresses an important compression problem: jointly allocating low-rank and sparse capacity across heterogeneous Transformer layers without updating the underlying weights.

The combination of RPCA decomposition and calibration-driven probabilistic selection is plausible. Table 1 reports consistent improvements over SparseGPT, WANDA, and BESA across five models; for LLaMA-2-7B, perplexity improves from BESA’s 6.60 to 6.25.
Experiments cover language modeling and downstream accuracy, with additional encoder-model comparisons and useful exploratory analyses of decomposition iterations and retained ranks.
weaknesses: The parameter-budget algorithm is inconsistent. Section 5.2.2 correctly assigns cost m+n to each retained singular direction, but subsequently projects onto the unweighted constraint 1ᵀs≤K. Equation (17) selects the top Pkeep mask variables despite their unequal costs. Neither operation guarantees the stated parameter budget, undermining confidence in comparisons at matched compression ratios.

The theoretical guarantees are unsupported. Theorem F.1 provides no meaningful derivation, recovery assumptions, or explicit dependence on the compression budget; invoking RPCA and PAC-Bayes does not establish the stated bound. Corollary F.3 omits the weight norms and Lipschitz assumptions needed to control error propagation through a Transformer. RPCA also does not generally guarantee the claimed orthogonality of its low-rank and sparse components.

The policy-gradient analysis overstates correctness. Updating the baseline with the current sampled loss before using it makes the baseline sample-dependent, invalidating the stated unbiasedness argument. The epsilon-modified score is also not the exact Bernoulli score. No convergence or variance evidence explains how the reported three iterations suffice for such a large selection space.

Experimental descriptions contain material contradictions. Table 4 identifies its model as LLaMA-7B, whereas the main text and adjacent configuration identify DeBERTaV3-base. Appendix D repeatedly describes 75% parameter retention as higher sparsity than the main 50% compression setting. These ambiguities prevent reliable interpretation of important comparisons.

The evidence does not isolate the main contribution. Budget-matched ablations of RPCA versus SVD initialization, learned versus fixed rank/sparsity allocation, and global versus layerwise optimization are missing. Table 3 changes rank and sparsity without matching total budgets. The main results are described as layerwise pruning despite the emphasis on global optimization, and the claimed global improvement lacks a detailed results table.

Practical efficiency claims lack measurements of peak memory, compression time, serialized storage including sparse indices, or inference latency. Parameter reduction alone does not establish deployment benefits for a low-rank-plus-unstructured-sparse representation. Direct composite-method comparisons on the evaluated LLMs are also absent; in Table 4, CAP without fine-tuning substantially trails LoSparse on MNLI.

Reproducibility remains insufficient despite Appendix C: the actual calibration context length, RPCA parameter values and stopping criteria, mask sampling counts, exact budget enforcement, and detailed encoder fine-tuning protocols are not specified. Stochastic results lack repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. Overall, the promising reported gains do not overcome the unresolved algorithmic and evaluation issues.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful compression problem: jointly allocating low-rank capacity and sparse corrections across layers without updating the underlying model weights.

Table 1 reports consistent improvements over SparseGPT, WANDA, and BESA across five LLaMA/LLaMA-2 configurations. For example, LLaMA-7B perplexity improves from BESA’s 6.86 to 6.61, and mean zero-shot accuracy increases from 63.13% to 64.29%.
The RPCA-iteration experiments and module-wise rank visualization provide useful exploratory evidence about decomposition quality and heterogeneous compression requirements.
weaknesses: The central parameter-budget mechanism is mathematically inconsistent. Section 5.2.2 correctly assigns a cost of m+n to each retained singular direction, but subsequently projects probabilities onto the unweighted constraint 1ᵀs≤K. Equation (17) then selects the top Pkeep mask entries despite their unequal parameter costs. Neither operation guarantees the stated parameter budget. Even a correctly weighted expectation constraint would require a separate budget-feasible rounding procedure.

The theoretical guarantees are unsupported. RPCA does not generally ensure the claimed orthogonality between its low-rank and sparse components. Theorem F.1 lacks the recovery assumptions, pruning-budget dependence, and derivation needed to connect RPCA and PAC-Bayes results to its weight-error bound. Corollary F.3 omits weight norms, activation bounds, and loss/network Lipschitz factors required to control error propagation through a Transformer. Lemma F.2 largely restates parameter counting without establishing capacity preservation or optimality.

Experimental descriptions contain consequential contradictions. Appendix D calls 75% parameter retention a higher-sparsity setting than the main 50% compression experiment, leaving the actual budget unclear. Table 4 identifies its experiment as zero-shot LLaMA-7B evaluation, whereas Section 6.1 and Table 5 identify the LoSparse comparison as DeBERTaV3-base; Table 4 also includes full fine-tuning. These discrepancies prevent confident interpretation of the comparisons.

The evidence does not isolate the proposed contribution. Table 3 varies thresholds and sparsity without matching total parameter budgets to CAP. There is no controlled comparison separating RPCA initialization, probabilistic selection, and global allocation on the principal LLM experiments. The claimed average 0.2 perplexity advantage of global over layer-wise pruning lacks a supporting results table and detailed protocol. Direct composite-method comparisons are confined to differently configured appendix experiments.

The global optimization procedure is insufficiently specified. The paper alternates between joint cross-layer optimization and sequential layer-wise pruning, without clearly identifying the procedure behind Table 1. Three policy-gradient iterations are reported without convergence evidence or clarification of mask samples per update. Reproduction details omit numerical RPCA settings, calibration context length, probability initialization, and a precise budget projection/rounding algorithm. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported despite stochastic mask optimization.

Practical efficiency claims lack measurements. There are no comparative compression-time, peak-memory, serialized-size, or inference-throughput results. Parameter counting excludes sparse-index storage, and actual acceleration depends on executing both low-rank and unstructured sparse operations. The qualitative claim that repeated RPCA decompositions take only a few minutes does not establish deployment benefits or scalability.

Novelty is primarily the combination of established RPCA and REINFORCE mechanisms. Such a combination could be useful, but the current ablations and comparisons do not establish a substantial advance. Claims of optimal pruning and globally optimal allocation exceed what the nonconvex stochastic procedure and presented evidence support.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful compression problem: jointly allocating low-rank capacity and sparse corrections across layers without updating the underlying model weights. Combining RPCA with calibration-driven mask selection is a plausible approach.

Table 1 reports consistent improvements over SparseGPT, WANDA, and BESA across five LLaMA/LLaMA-2 models. For example, at nominal 50% compression, LLaMA-2-7B perplexity improves from BESA’s 6.60 to 6.25, and mean zero-shot accuracy increases from 64.92 to 65.33.
The experiments include models up to 30B parameters, language modeling and downstream tasks, and useful exploratory analyses of RPCA iterations and retained ranks.
weaknesses: The budget enforcement is mathematically inconsistent. Section 5.2.2 correctly assigns each retained singular direction a cost of m+n parameters, but subsequently projects onto the unweighted constraint 1ᵀs ≤ K. Equation (17) then selects the top Pkeep mask entries despite their unequal costs. Neither operation guarantees the stated parameter budget. An explicit cost-aware projection and discrete selection algorithm, together with achieved parameter counts, are necessary to validate the compression comparisons.

The theoretical guarantees are unsupported. RPCA does not generally ensure the claimed orthogonality between its low-rank and sparse components. Theorem F.1 invokes RPCA recovery and PAC-Bayes without specifying recovery assumptions, a posterior/prior, or a derivation connecting calibration loss to matrix reconstruction error; its bound also lacks explicit dependence on the retained budget. Corollary F.3 omits weight norms and Lipschitz factors needed to control error propagation through a Transformer. These statements do not establish the claimed guarantees.

The central global-optimization contribution is insufficiently demonstrated. Section 6.1 describes Table 1 as using layer-wise probabilistic pruning after global RPCA, although decompositions are performed independently per matrix. The claimed average 0.2-perplexity benefit from global pruning has no accompanying comparison table. There is no controlled, equal-budget ablation separating RPCA, policy-gradient selection, and global allocation; Table 3 varies ranks and sparsities without matching total parameter counts.

Appendix experiments contain material reporting inconsistencies. Table 4 identifies its model as LLaMA-7B with zero-shot evaluation, whereas the main text and Table 5 identify the LoSparse comparison as DeBERTaV3-base. Tables 6–7 and Appendix D specify 75% parameter retention while describing this as higher sparsity than the main 50% compression setting. These contradictions leave the model identities, evaluation protocols, and compression levels uncertain.

Evidence for superiority over composite approximation methods is limited. LoSparse and LPAF are compared only in smaller-model appendix experiments with incompletely specified training protocols. In Table 4, CAP without fine-tuning substantially trails LoSparse on MNLI and QNLI; the strongest CAP results require full parameter fine-tuning. Thus, the broad claim of outperforming composite methods without weight updates is not established. The cited one-shot sparse-plus-low-rank method SLIM is not evaluated.

Practical efficiency and reproducibility remain insufficiently supported. There are no measured inference latency, peak memory, serialized storage, or comparative compression-time results, and parameter counts omit sparse-index overhead. Appendix C provides a file outline and generic execution instructions but leaves essential settings unclear, including numerical RPCA defaults, probability initialization, calibration context length, and mask-sampling details. Only three policy-gradient iterations are reported, without convergence evidence or variability across seeds.
